snippet.title: I'm Bored!  Let's Go On A Ham Radio Adventure!
snippet.description:
I was bored out of my mind on Friday.  The urge to play radio was growing stronger by the minute.  I've got new gear I want to play with and an antenna that I made months ago (if not longer) that I've never used.  But I didn't want to go to any of the parks around me.  I've activated them all already.  I wanted something new.  So I set out on a quest for a new park.  Far from home.  One I'd never even heard of before.  It was beautiful.  In this video I take you along my journey, show you the park, my setup, my antenna, everything but the contacts.  Analytics show that once I get on the air in a POTA video, most people tune out.  Myself included.  What is interesting to me is the journey, the setup, the gear, location, and the results.  Hopefully it is to you too.  Gone are the days where watching someone make POTA contacts is considered exciting (unless it's live, perhaps).  Not saying I'll never show making contacts in a video again, but perhaps this format will prove more engaging.  It's certainly more fun for me to make.  Let me know what you think.

snippet.title: Radioddity HF-010: The 10 Band Vertical That Comes With Everything
snippet.description:
SPONSORED VIDEO: Radioddity sent Everyday Ham an HF-010 Portable HF Antenna kit, so Jim (N8JRD) opened the case, walked every single piece in it, and then took the whole thing to the park for a real POTA activation.
Get the HF-010 and save $15 with code EVERYDAYHAM: https://www.radioddity.com/products/radioddity-hf-010?ref=EVERYDAYHAM

The pitch on the HF-010 is completeness. Everything you need to walk into a park and start calling CQ is already in the bag: whip, ground spike, extension rods, sliding tuning coil, a separate fixed coil for 80 meters, radials on spools, coax on its own winder, a folding tripod, and a few extras Jim didn't expect to find in there. Throw it in the truck with a radio and you're set.

Jim goes through all of it on the table before anything gets assembled, which is the part nobody else seems to cover. What each piece does, why the threads are the way they are, what the sliding coil is actually doing when you move it, and which pieces are built better than he expected. The tuning coil in particular is smooth, enclosed against weather, and quick to move between bands.

Then it goes up at Island Lake Recreation Area, US-3315, for a genuine activation on 20 meters at 100 watts. The SWR number surprised him, and the first contact out of the gate was a park to park all the way into Texas.

snippet.title: How Do Submarines Communicate Underwater?
snippet.description:
Underwater communication is surprisingly difficult. Seawater absorbs most ordinary radio signals, forcing submarines to rely on specialized technologies and carefully designed communication methods.

In this video, we explore how submarines stay connected beneath the surface, from extremely low-frequency radio to underwater acoustic communication, and why different methods are needed at different depths.

snippet.title: This was supposed to be a two-metre summit.
snippet.description:
Fourth summit in four days. One contact, then two, then seven. This one gave me thirteen and I still can't tell you why.

I changed nothing on purpose. Same wire, same 49:1, same knot as the day before on Sulzspitze. What was different is that I nearly didn't put it up at all.

Halfway up, my wife left the trail to climb B'schießer on her own. No plan, no discussion, no camera with her. That left me on the ridge with all four kids, and by the time we got to the top I had talked myself out of HF completely. The summit is narrow, there is a drop on one side, and I had four children to keep away from it. I said on camera that this one would be 2m only.

I put the wire up anyway. Thirteen contacts on twenty metres, three of them summit to summit, one with a YL, and the biggest pileup I have had.

Everything you see from the summit was filmed by the kids. I was operating, they had the camera.

The only thing I did differently from the first three days is height. The far end went up on the fishing rod on the highest ground I could reach, maybe two metres above where it sat before, and the wire ran as a sloper. That is all. Second time in a row it worked, and again I measured nothing.

One more thing I am not sure about. Kühgundkopf is a German reference, but the summit sits on the border and I sat on the Austrian side, so I signed OE/HF2LT/P. Is that how you would have done it? I said on camera that it depends which side you put the antenna on. I am not convinced that is right.

So: is two metres of pole height really worth this much, or was the wire always fine and the first three days were me? I would like to know which one it is.

KÜHGUNDKOPF · DL/AL-049 · 1907 m · 8 points · Allgäuer Alpen, on the Austrian border · operating as OE/HF2LT/P

Result: 13 QSO, 3 S2S - activated
Band / mode: 20m SSB
Log and full activation history: https://sotl.as/summits/DL/AL-049

RADIO
Yaesu FT-857D
End-fed half-wave, 49:1 transformer, choke balun
Fishing rod, far end on the high point, wire run as a sloper
LiFePO4 9 Ah
Handhelds and PMR for the family

We're a family that carries a radio up mountains. Four kids, one licence between us so far, and a lot of arguments about who gets to hold the log.

Instagram: @fota_sota
QRZ: HF2LT
familyontheair@gmail.com

In 1912, American ham radio operators were publicly blamed for people dying on the Titanic. The story was that amateurs clogged the airwaves so badly the ship's calls for help couldn't get through. You can still find versions of it today, in encyclopedia entries and on government websites.

snippet.title: SOTA Activation: Impressions of the Yaesu FTX-1 @ 14,115' + S2S Contact!
snippet.description:
Hey Everyone! 

In this video, we head up to the summit of Pikes Peak for my first official Summits on the Air (SOTA) activation. The forecast called for temps in the 50s with light winds… but reality on the mountaintop had other plans. When we reached the summit, it was 42° and dropping fast. By the end of the activation, the wind had picked up considerably and I quickly learned I did not bring the right gear for 37° conditions! Nonetheless, we made the absolute best out of the activation and walked away with around 18 official contacts and many more that were unofficial because I made the contact outside the SOTA activation zone. 

Main Takeaways for my Next SOTA:
- Dress warmer and shed layers as needed
- Bring a small table for the Yaesu FTX‑1 Field
- Retire the rubber‑ducky antenna and run a 3‑element yagi
- Stick with the FTX‑1 so I can operate SSB reliably on 144.200 MHz

Thank you to everyone who participated!

SOTA Spotting: https://sotawatch.sota.org.uk/en/

00:00 - Intro
04:25 - View of the FTX-1 and scenery
06:50 - Pulling over and showing mobile antennas
07:50 - Mile Marker 7
10:00 - Working a station on 146.520 by KDEN
11:42 - Listening to my 2M beacon in Kansas
12:01 - Nearing the summit!
12:34 - At the summit!
13:00 - Beginning the activation, round 1
21:24 - Warming up and watching Superman run by!
21:30 - Starting round 2
33:37 - Round 3 of the activations
40:50 - Outro

If you have questions, suggestions, or whatever the case may be, please feel free to get in 
contact with me.

73, 
Chad 
NØYK
